summary: This standards-track document describes how to convey the path setup type in PCEP messages. A Path Computation Element can compute traffic-engineered paths, which were traditionally set up with RSVP-TE, but other setup methods are possible. It lets PCEP say which method applies.

plainLanguage.summary: When a path computer works out a route for a traffic engineering tunnel, it has to say how that tunnel should be built. This RFC adds a way for the two ends to agree on that, and a way for each to say which methods it understands before any path is requested.

subtitle: How PCEP peers announce and select the method used to set up a traffic engineering path, beyond RSVP-TE.

tldr.problem: PCEP was built on the assumption that traffic engineering paths are label switched and set up with RSVP-TE, but the architecture allows other setup methods, and PCEP had no way to say which one was in use.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two new TLVs: a PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV that a peer announces at session setup to list the methods it supports, and a PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV that names the method for one particular LSP.
tldr.outcome: The result is that a PCC and a PCE can use a setup method other than RSVP-TE and still agree on it, with RSVP-TE remaining the default when nothing else is indicated. RFC 8408 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8664.

facts.label: PCErr error type
facts.value: 21, invalid traffic engineering path setup type

today: RFC 8408 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8664. It defines only the RSVP-TE path setup type and leaves new types to the documents that introduce them, so the two objects and the error codes it registers are the ones in use.

sections.title: Why PCEP Needs a Path Setup Type
sections.content:
RFC 5440 describes the PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) for communication between a Path Computation Client (PCC) and a Path Computation Element (PCE), or between one PCE and another. A PCC requests, from a PCE, a path subject to various constraints and optimization criteria. The PCE responds to the PCC with a hop-by-hop path in an Explicit Route Object (ERO), and the PCC uses the ERO to set up the path in the network.

RFC 8231 specifies extensions that allow a PCC to delegate its LSPs to a PCE, so that the PCE can update their state, for instance by sending a new ERO that the PCC uses to reroute the LSP in a make-before-break fashion. RFC 8281 specifies a mechanism that allows a PCE to dynamically instantiate an LSP on a PCC.

So far, PCEP and its extensions have assumed that the traffic engineering paths are label switched and are established with the RSVP-TE signalling protocol. However, other methods of LSP setup are possible in the PCE architecture. This document generalizes PCEP to allow other LSP setup methods to be used, and defines two new TLVs to facilitate it.

The PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV allows a PCEP speaker to announce which LSP setup methods it supports when the PCEP session is established. The PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV allows a PCEP speaker to specify which setup method should be used for a given LSP. When multiple path setup types are deployed in a network, a given PCEP session may have to support more than one at the same time, so a PCEP speaker uses the PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV to explicitly indicate the intended path setup type in the appropriate PCEP messages, unless the path setup type is RSVP-TE, which is assumed when no other setup type is indicated. That is so that both the PCC and the PCE can take the necessary steps to set up the path.

This document defines a path setup type code for RSVP-TE. When a new path setup type other than RSVP-TE is introduced, the document that specifies it will define a path setup type code and, optionally, a sub-TLV for it.
sections.plainLanguage: PCEP worked out routes for tunnels that were always built with RSVP-TE. This RFC lets the same protocol carry a tunnel built a different way, by agreeing on the method first.

sections.title: Terms
sections.content:
The document uses a short set of terms. An ERO is an Explicit Route Object, the hop-by-hop path a PCE hands back. A PCC is a Path Computation Client, the element that asks for a path. A PCE is a Path Computation Element, the element that computes one. PCEP is the PCE Communication Protocol itself. A PST is a Path Setup Type, the method used to set the path up in the network. A TLV is a Type, Length, and Value.

The two new objects are named after those terms: the PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV carries a list of the PSTs a speaker supports, and the PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV carries the single PST that applies to one LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: The only new term is "path setup type": the name for the method used to build a tunnel, such as RSVP-TE.

sections.title: The Path Setup Type Capability TLV
sections.content:
A PCEP speaker indicates which path setup types it supports during the PCEP initialization phase. When the session is created, it sends an Open message with an OPEN object containing the PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV, whose type is 34. Its Reserved field MUST be set to zero by the sender and MUST be ignored by the receiver.

The rest of the TLV holds a count and a list. The Num of PSTs field is the number of path setup types in the following list, excluding padding. The list itself holds the supported types, each a single byte, and duplicate entries in the list MUST be ignored. The speaker MUST pad the list with zeros so that it is a multiple of four bytes in length. This document defines one value: PST 0 means the path is set up using the RSVP-TE signalling protocol. Optional sub-TLVs may follow, each associated with exactly one path setup type and each obeying the TLV formatting rules of RFC 5440.

The speaker has to check that the TLV is correctly formatted. With no sub-TLVs, the Length field must equal four bytes plus the size of the path setup type list, excluding padding. With sub-TLVs, it must equal four bytes plus the size of the list rounded up to the nearest multiple of four, plus the size of the appended sub-TLVs, excluding any padding in the final sub-TLV. The Num of PSTs field must be greater than zero. A speaker that receives a TLV violating these rules MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 10, reception of an invalid object, and Error-value 11, malformed object, and MUST close the PCEP session. If an OPEN object carries more than one of these TLVs, all but the first instance MUST be ignored.

The absence of the TLV is equivalent to one holding a single path setup type value of 0 and no sub-TLVs. A speaker MAY omit it if the only type it supports is RSVP-TE, and SHOULD include it if it supports others.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end of the session lists the methods it can build tunnels with, as a short list of numbers. If a reader does not recognise the list at all, it ignores it and assumes the older method.

sections.title: The Path Setup Type TLV
sections.content:
When a PCEP session is used to set up traffic engineering paths using different methods, the PCE and the PCC must be aware of the method used. The PCE must be able to specify paths in the correct format, and the PCC must be able to take the control-plane and forwarding-plane actions appropriate to the path setup type.

The PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV is an optional TLV associated with the Request Parameters (RP) object of RFC 5440 and the Stateful PCE Request Parameters (SRP) object of RFC 8231. Its type is 28, and its Reserved field MUST be set to zero. The one-byte PST field holds the path setup type, defined exactly as for the capability TLV.

The absence of the TLV is equivalent to one with a PST value of 0, meaning the path is set up using RSVP-TE. A speaker MAY omit it if the type is RSVP-TE. If the RP or SRP object contains more than one PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV, only the first MUST be processed and the rest MUST be ignored. A speaker that does not recognise the TLV ignores it in accordance with RFC 5440 and uses RSVP-TE to set up the path.
sections.plainLanguage: The second object is smaller: one number saying which method to use for one particular tunnel, carried inside the request for that tunnel.

sections.title: How the Two Ends Agree
sections.content:
During the initialization phase, a PCEP speaker that receives a PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV from its peer MUST assume that the peer supports only the types listed in it. If the speaker and its peer have no path setup type in common, the speaker MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 21, invalid traffic engineering path setup type, and Error-value 2, mismatched path setup type, and close the PCEP session. If the peer sent no capability TLV, the speaker MUST infer that the peer supports at least RSVP-TE, and MAY infer that it supports others, though the means of inference are outside the scope of this document.

When a PCC sends a PCReq message, it MUST include the PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV in the RP object, unless the intended type is RSVP-TE, in which case it MAY omit it. If the PCE is capable of expressing the path in a format appropriate to the intended type, it MUST use the appropriate ERO format in the PCRep message. When a PCE sends a PCRep, it MUST include the TLV in the RP object, unless the type is RSVP-TE. If the PCE does not support the intended type, it MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 21 and Error-value 1, unsupported path setup type, and close the session. If the types in the request and the reply do not match, the PCC MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 21 and Error-value 2 and close the session.

The same pattern applies to the stateful messages. When a stateful PCE sends a PCUpd or a PCInitiate message, it MUST include the TLV in the SRP object unless the type is RSVP-TE, and a PCC that does not support that type MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 21 and Error-value 1 and close the session. When a PCC sends a PCRpt message, it MUST include the TLV in the SRP object unless the type is RSVP-TE, and it MUST include the SRP object even when the SRP-ID-number is the reserved value of 0x00000000. If the report was triggered by a PCUpd or PCInitiate message, the type the PCC indicates MUST match the one the stateful PCE intended; if it does not, the PCE MUST send a PCErr message with Error-Type 21 and Error-value 2 and close the session.
sections.plainLanguage: If the two ends do not share a method, the session is closed with an error. If they do, each message names the method it is about, so neither end builds the tunnel the wrong way.

sections.title: Manageability Considerations
sections.content:
This document generalizes PCEP to allow path setup methods other than RSVP-TE to be used by the network, although it defines no new path setup types beyond RSVP-TE itself. It is possible that a given network will use several methods at once, and that not all devices will support the same set of methods. Managing networks that combine multiple path setup methods may therefore raise challenges from a configuration and observability point of view.

Each document that defines a new path setup type in the "PCEP Path Setup Types" registry must include a Manageability Considerations section, and that section must explain how operators can manage PCEP with the new type. It must address five questions. What are the criteria for when devices will use the new path setup type in PCEP, and how can the operator control this? How can the network be migrated to the new path setup type, and are there backwards-compatibility issues that operators need to be aware of? Are paths set up using the new type intended to coexist with other paths over the long term, and if so, how is that situation managed with PCEP? How can operators verify the correct operation of PCEP in the network with respect to the new type, and which fault conditions must be reported to the operators? Are there any existing management interfaces, such as YANG models, that must be extended to model the operation of PCEP in the network with respect to the new type?
sections.plainLanguage: Each new setup method has to come with a note on how operators run it: when it is used, how to migrate to it, how it coexists with the old one, how to check it works, and what has to be added to the management models.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations described in RFC 5440 and RFC 8281 are applicable to this specification. No additional security measure is required.

The RFC then adds one note. If the security mechanisms of RFC 5440 and RFC 8281 are not used, the protocol described in this document could be attacked in a new way. An attacker using a TCP man-in-the-middle attack could inject error messages into the PCEP session when a particular path setup type is, or is not, used. Doing this could potentially force the use of a specific path setup type, which may allow the attacker to subsequently attack a weakness in that type.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is required, but there is a new way to attack an unprotected session: an attacker could push both ends towards one setup method and then exploit a weakness in it.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Two code points are allocated in the "PCEP TLV Type Indicators" registry: value 28 for PATH-SETUP-TYPE and value 34 for PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY.

A new sub-registry is created within the "Path Computation Element Protocol (PCEP) Numbers" registry, called "PCEP Path Setup Types", with IETF Review as the allocation policy. Its first value is 0, meaning that the path is set up using the RSVP-TE signalling protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the lists of object numbers and of setup methods. This RFC adds two object numbers and the first method, RSVP-TE, numbered zero.
